findings.reason: without the owner module in the write paths, or a reading that carries its arm, the node cannot satisfy cases 1 and 3 except by a second liveness implementation, which is the defect §4 exists to prevent.
findings.text: §8 requires the result to distinguish a live recorded pid from the session-walk arm and from a placed run, but `record_process_alive` answers only `bool | None` (`reckon/crew/process_liveness.py:300`, returning at `:380`); the arm is decided inside it (placement at `:356`, session walk at `:377-379`, start-time reuse check at `:337-347`), and `reckon/crew/process_liveness.py` is not among §8's write paths, so a node must either duplicate the liveness decision in `crew_run_commands.py`/`claims.py` — two implementations of one truth that drift the moment the reuse check changes — or edit outside its fence.

findings.reason: a coordinator told "the next launch mounts them" while liveness was never read is exactly the false assurance the field is being added to remove, so the field needs the "liveness could not be read on this host" arm the plan's own §6 already uses.
findings.text: §8 says that "when no worker is alive, it says the next resume or launch mounts them", but the reading it names is tri-state: `record_process_alive` also answers `None` when the record names no process or the scheduler cannot be queried (`reckon/crew/process_liveness.py:352-358`, with `process_alive` returning `None` for a missing pid), and `widen_claim` treats anything other than `True` as "not alive" (`reckon/crew/claims.py:106`); the deliverable collapses that unproven reading into a positive statement.

response_events.note: §8 grants reckon/crew/process_liveness.py and has it expose one reading that carries its arm (recorded pid alive, session walk, placed run, unknown); record_process_alive keeps its boolean by reading that one function, so there is one liveness decision
